name: ALG3-CDG (CDG-Id)
aliases: congenital disorder of glycosylation type Id

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: An N-linked type I CDG caused by ALG3 deficiency, a mannosyltransferase in endoplasmic reticulum assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide
Presents with severe developmental delay, profound microcephaly, hypotonia and drug-resistant seizures
Ophthalmological anomalies including optic atrophy and cortical visual impairment are commonly reported
Skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphism, feeding difficulties and failure to thrive are part of the phenotype
Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing shows a type I pattern from under-occupancy of N-glycan sites
Coagulation and hepatic abnormalities may accompany the neurological picture
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; ALG3 sequencing confirms the diagnosis
reference.pathophysiology: ALG3 encodes a dolichol-phosphate-mannose-dependent mannosyltransferase acting on the endoplasmic reticulum-luminal face during assembly of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide precursor. Loss of function yields a truncated precursor that is transferred inefficiently to protein, leaving N-linked sites under-occupied and generating a type I transferrin pattern. Because the block is in precursor assembly rather than glycan processing, the disorder is classified as type I. Widespread hypoglycosylation impairs neuronal, ocular and other glycoproteins, producing the severe neurodevelopmental and multisystem phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Other type I CDG subtypes (e.g. ALG1-CDG, ALG12-CDG, PMM2-CDG)
Genetic causes of severe microcephaly with epileptic encephalopathy
Congenital causes of optic atrophy with developmental delay
additionalInvestigations: Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry showing a type I pattern
Neuroimaging for microcephaly and structural change
Ophthalmological assessment including optic nerve evaluation
redFlags: Failure to thrive with multi-organ involvement
reference.prognosis: ALG3-CDG is a severe disorder with profound neurodevelopmental disability and significant early morbidity and mortality; prognosis is generally poor and correlates with residual enzyme activity and complication burden.
pitfalls: Attributing the transferrin abnormality to secondary causes without genetic confirmation
Assuming disease-modifying therapy exists when only supportive care is available
Missing associated ophthalmological complications that need surveillance
references: Scriver's OMMBID, congenital disorders of glycosylation
Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, disorders of glycosylation
management: No curative or disease-specific therapy exists; care is supportive and directed at the multisystem consequences of hypoglycosylation
Control drug-resistant seizures with antiseizure medication tailored under paediatric neurology guidance
Optimise nutrition and growth with dietitian-led feeding support and gastrostomy feeding for feeding difficulties and failure to thrive
Support development and hypotonia with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy
Provide ophthalmology input and low-vision support for optic atrophy and cortical visual impairment
Monitor and correct coagulation and hepatic abnormalities, seeking haematology advice before procedures
Coordinate multidisciplinary metabolic, neurology and rehabilitation care with early palliative involvement given the severe prognosis
Offer genetic counselling, prenatal testing and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
